newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-HEADLEY SHINES ON ENGLAND DEBUT.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-HEADLEY SHINES ON ENGLAND DEBUT.

text.p: MANCHESTER, England, July 3 (Reuter) Paceman Dean Headley's fine test debut and Alec Stewart's safe catching had Australia in trouble after two sessions of the third test against England at Old Trafford on Thursday.
The touring team, trailing 1-0 in the six-match series, were 162 for seven at tea on the opening day.
Wicketkeeper Stewart held five catches and Headley captured three for 47 from 18 overs, having snared openers Mark Taylor and Matthew Elliott, then Michael Bevan.

The Kent pace bowler made cricket history even before his first delivery, his selection ahead of Devon Malcolm and Mike Smith making his family the first to produce three generations of test cricketers.
Grandfather George and father Ron both played for the West Indies, as batsmen.
Dean Headley's 11th ball produced a wicket, Taylor edging to slip for two -- his third single-figure score in four innings of this series.

Darren Gough, bowling with fire and economy, had Greg Blewett playing on for eight in his opening spell and Mark Ealham, though less accurate, lured Mark Waugh into offering a catch behind for 12. That left the Australians atruggling at 42 for three.
Waugh has failed to make a good score in four innings so far and so has Bevan, who was also caught behind, in his case off Headley for seven.

Elliott lasted longer, and was unlucky to become Stewart's third victim, the ball appearing to come off his elbow. He made 40 and was top-scorer until Steve Waugh passed him shortly before a mid-afternoon break for rain that lasted 40 minutes.

Waugh, the other batsman who had not made runs in the series to date, reached 50 soon after the resumption, off 73 balls. He lost Shane Warne to Stewart's fifth catch for three, but was unbeaten on 70 at tea, with Paul Reiffel not out one.

Taylor had a difficult decision to make after winning the toss on an overcast morning. The pitch was damp, with bare patches as well as some green ones, and seemed likely to favour bowlers rather than batsmen from the start.
Taylor may or may not have been aware that no team had ever won a test at Old Trafford after inserting the opposition.
